add-sub-like.why: The denominator names the size of the pieces. Adding three eighths to two eighths gives five eighths because you are counting pieces of the same size — and the size does not change when you count them.
traps: Never add the denominators. ~\f{1}{4} + \f{1}{4}~ is ~\f{2}{4} = \f{1}{2}~, not ~\f{2}{8}~.

add-sub-unlike.why: You cannot add pieces of different sizes, so first rewrite both fractions with a common denominator. The least common denominator keeps the numbers small, but any common denominator gives the right answer.
traps: Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by too. Changing one alone changes the value.

add-sub-mixed.why: Two routes work: convert both to improper fractions, or handle wholes and parts separately. Converting first is a few more strokes of the pen but far harder to get wrong, especially when subtraction needs a borrow.
traps: ~3\f{1}{4} - 1\f{3}{4}~ needs a borrow: the fraction parts alone would give a negative. Converting to ~\f{13}{4} - \f{7}{4}~ avoids the problem entirely.

mult-fractions.why: Multiply straight across — and notice that 'of' means multiply, so half of a third is ~\f{1}{2} \times \f{1}{3}~. This is the operation where the area picture is essential: it is a rectangle half as wide and a third as tall.
traps: Multiplying by a number below 1 makes things *smaller*. That feels wrong if you learned that multiplication makes things bigger.

div-fractions.why: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal. The reason: ~6 \div \f{1}{2}~ asks how many halves fit in 6, and twelve do. Dividing by a number below 1 makes the answer bigger, because you are counting smaller pieces.
traps: Flip the *second* fraction only, and only after you have rewritten the division as a multiplication.

fraction-of-quantity.why: Finding a fraction of an amount is the most common real use of fractions: divide by the denominator, multiply by the numerator. Going the other way — recovering the whole from a part — means dividing by the fraction.
traps: If ~\f{2}{3}~ of a number is 18, the number is 27, not 12. Find one part first (9), then take three of them.

complex-fractions.why: A fraction whose parts are themselves fractions looks alarming and is not: the main bar still means divide. Rewrite it as a division and multiply by the reciprocal. This exact pattern reappears throughout algebra and in every rate-of-a-rate.
traps: Identify the main bar first. ~\f{1}{\f{2}{3}}~ is 1.5, but ~\f{\f{1}{2}}{3}~ is about 0.167.
